16.5.7.4 Halogenation

Alkenes readily add halogen (chlorine and bromine) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or carbon disulfide to form vicinal dihalides (or vic-dihalides). Vicinal dichlorides and dibromides are unstable at high temperature, while vicinal diiodides are unstable even at room temperature. The reactivity of various halogens with alkenes decrease down the group. Reaction involves in the formation of a cyclic halonium ion. For example ethene upon reaction with bromine in inert solvent, form 1, 2 dibromoethane (ethylene dibromide).

The bromination of alkenes provides a useful test for the presence of a double bond in the molecules. When dilute solution of bromine is added to a compound containing carbon-carbon double bond, the colour of bromine rapidly discharges as the colorless dibromo compound is formed. This is called bromine water test.

Tidbit

Geminal dihalides (or gem-dihalide) have both halogen atoms attached to the same carbon atom whereas vicinal dihalides (or vic-dihalides) have their two halogen atoms attached to two adjacent carbon atoms.

16.5.7.5 Halohydration

When alkene is reacted with halogen in an inert solvent, vic-dihalides are formed, because halide ion is the only nucleophile available for reaction with the intermediate cyclic halonium ion. However if the reaction is performed in aqueous solution, water can also act as nucleophile and attack on cyclic halonium ion to form halo-alcohols, commonly known as halohydrin. For example; ethene when reacted with aqueous bromine, forms 2-bromoethanol, commonly called ethylene bromohydrin.

16.5.7.6 Epoxidation

Alkenes on reaction with peroxyacids (or peracid) yield cyclic ethers called epoxides (or oxiranes). This process in known as epoxidation. The most commonly used peracid, is peracetic acid. For example ethylene when treated with peracetic acid form ethylene oxide (epoxyethane or oxirane).

On industrial scale, ethylene oxide is prepared, by air oxidation of ethene with silver oxide catalyst at 300°C.

16.5.7.7 Ozonolysis

When ozone (O₃) gas is passed through a solution of alkene in an inert solvent, at low temperature (−80°C), an addition product molozonide is formed. This molozonide rearranges rapidly to form ozonide.

In case of asymmetric alkenes, the reaction follows the Markovnikov’s rule. For example hydration of propene gives mainly isopropyl alcohol (propane–2–ol).

16.5.7.4 Halogenation

Alkenes readily add halogen (chlorine and bromine) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or carbon disulfide to form vicinal dihalides (or vic-dihalides). Vicinal dichlorides and dibromides are unstable at high temperature, while vicinal diiodides are unstable even at room temperature. The reactivity of various halogens with alkenes decrease down the group. Reaction involves in the formation of a cyclic halonium ion. For example ethene upon reaction with bromine in inert solvent, form 1, 2 dibromoethane (ethylene dibromide).

The bromination of alkenes provides a useful test for the presence of a double bond in the molecules. When dilute solution of bromine is added to a compound containing carbon-carbon double bond, the colour of bromine rapidly discharges as the colorless dibromo compound is formed. This is called bromine water test.

Tidbit

Geminal dihalides (or gem-dihalide) have both halogen atoms attached to the same carbon atom whereas vicinal dihalides (or vic-dihalides) have their two halogen atoms attached to two adjacent carbon atoms.

16.5.7.5 Halohydration

When alkene is reacted with halogen in an inert solvent, vic-dihalides are formed, because halide ion is the only nucleophile available for reaction with the intermediate cyclic halonium ion. However if the reaction is performed in aqueous solution, water can also act as nucleophile and attack on cyclic halonium ion to form halo-alcohols, commonly known as halohydrin. For example; ethene when reacted with aqueous bromine, forms 2-bromoethanol, commonly called ethylene bromohydrin.

Self-assessment

Predict the product of bromohydration of but-2-ene and write the complete reaction.

16.5.7.6 Epoxidation

Alkenes on reaction with peroxyacids (or peracid) yield cyclic ethers called epoxides (or oxiranes). This process in known as epoxidation. The most commonly used peracid, is peracetic acid. For example ethylene when treated with peracetic acid form ethylene oxide (epoxyethane or oxirane).

On industrial scale, ethylene oxide is prepared, by air oxidation of ethene with silver oxide catalyst at 300°C.

16.5.7.7 Ozonolysis

When ozone (O₃) gas is passed through a solution of alkene in an inert solvent, at low temperature (−80°C), an addition product molozonide is formed. This molozonide rearranges rapidly to form ozonide.
